blocks.text: Quantifiers in predicate logic describe how many objects satisfy a condition. They let us make general statements, or statements about particular objects, such as 'All students are hardworking' or 'Some books are interesting'. Quantifiers make predicate logic more powerful than propositional logic and help represent knowledge clearly and precisely.

blocks.title: Tidbit
blocks.text: Quantifiers such as 'for all' and 'there exists' help us express general rules or possibilities clearly.

blocks.caption: The two quantifiers
rows: The statement is true for every object in the set
For all x, x > 0: every x is greater than 0
The statement is true for at least one object in the set
There exists x such that x is even: at least one x is even

blocks.text: The universal quantifier makes general statements about every object in a domain; it is important in mathematics and proofs, because it says that no object in the set breaks the statement. The existential quantifier is used when a condition is met by some object, not necessarily all; it expresses possibilities and specific examples (Fig 2.8).

blocks.alt: Two boxes of fifteen circles each. Left, marked with the universal symbol and 'for all': every circle is green; caption: for all x, P(x), every x satisfies P. Right, marked with the existential symbol and 'there exists': only one circle is green and the rest are empty; caption: there exists x, P(x), at least one x satisfies P. Green means the predicate P(x) is true for that object.
blocks.caption: The universal and existential quantifiers (original diagram after Fig 2.8).
blocks.long_description: 'For all' needs every object to pass; one failure makes it false. 'There exists' needs just one object to pass.

blocks.text: Quantifiers are combined with predicates to make clear statements: 'for all x, P(x)' means P(x) is true for every x, and 'there exists x, P(x)' means P(x) is true for at least one x. They can also be used together: 'for all x, there exists y such that y > x' means that for every number x there is some number y bigger than it.
